Reading to Write: Joining a Conversation

🖼️ Framing Our Work

One way to sustain literacy routines is to help students move from entering a text to entering a conversation among texts. In the fall, we explored strategies like They Say / I Say and Say–Mean–Matter to support students in noticing other voices and responding with their own ideas. This module builds on that foundation by introducing practices that help students read across multiple texts, recognize differing perspectives, and consider how writers position themselves in relation to others.

📝What to Expect

In this module, you will:

✅ Revisit the idea of argument as conversation by exploring how writers respond to and build on one another’s ideas across multiple texts

✅ Learn how to use the Atwoodian Table to help students listen to, sort, and compare perspectives as they join a conversation in progress

✅ Reflect on how these practices can support students in reading across texts, synthesizing ideas, and preparing to contribute their own thinking

✅ Earn the Joining a Conversation discussion badge for contributing your Atwoodian Table and reflections in the discussion

✅ Earn the Joining a Conversation microcredential by reflecting with your facilitator on how you might adapt the Atwoodian Table lesson sequence for your students, including sharing a draft or classroom example

🧭 Explore and Learn

The fall online course modules introduced the idea of argument as a conversation through the They Say / I Say and Say-Mean-Matter frameworks. Before responding in any conversation, we listen carefully to what others are saying, recognize other people’s perspectives, and then reply with our own ideas. Another way to understand this concept is through Kenneth Burke’s metaphorical parlor. Read through the resource below and consider the relationship between argument writing and conversation.

In Rewriting: How to Do Things with Text, Joseph Harris serves as a host to the Burkean Parlor, expanding on the idea that academic writing is a kind of conversation made in relation to others. Harris welcomes a writer to join a conversation in progress this way:

One of our goals for student writers is the self-driven exploration of issues that are important to them. Through inquiry, they can step into a discussion among authorities found in sources, take a position, and join the ongoing conversation.

One way students can join a conversation in progress is to be invited to a metaphorical table where they can “chat” with various stakeholders about an issue. Students read and process different viewpoints, then “pull up a chair” to the table and contribute their own voices to a multi-perspective argument. The abstract concept of a conversation among sources can seem more concrete when students follow the table metaphor to support their note-taking. This approach has been named the “Atwoodian Table” after its creator, Robin Atwood, a National Writing Project teacher-leader.

Check out the slideshow below, which provides an introduction to the Atwoodian Table and a sample lesson you might use with your students. The lesson sequence features excerpts with different viewpoints on one issue: Should fancy restaurants ban children? Links are provided to the full-length texts for further exploration of the topic.


Experience the metaphor in action! Create your own Atwoodian Table by working through the lesson sequence below, which features excerpts focused on the topic of Toddlers and Technology. As you read through the sources, you will engage and “hear” the conversations that authorities are already having about the topic. Click here to make a copy of the lesson.

💬 Try and Share

When you finish creating your table based on the excerpts about toddlers and technology, take a picture of your completed table and upload it to the Joining a Conversation Discussion. Include a comment or two about your experience as well as your thoughts about how you might use this in your own classroom.

Be sure to respond to the posts of others!

The Joining a Conversation discussion badge is automatically awarded when you post to the discussion and respond to 2 other posts in the discussion.

Not only did I enjoy doing this task myself, but I can definitely see its value in my classroom! We are in the middle of a research-based inquiry unit with my English 3 students (mock trial, create a podcast, write an essay, etc.), and I wish I had done this with them beforehand. In reality, every "seat" at the table has different experiences and morals that result in unique perspectives. I'm going to plan to do this activity with them before their last assignment in the unit: the essay. I really think this mindset of "joining at the table" will help them see the value in finding evidence and integrating it in a way that contributes to the overall existing argument.
